Cadence. A concluding harmonic phrase that signals the end of a musical phrase, section, or entire piece. It is the melodic and harmonic equivalent of punctuation, with different types conveying finality, pause, or continuity, and it serves as a fundamental punctuation mark in tonal music.

The authentic cadence, also called the perfect cadence, moves from the dominant chord to the tonic, the strongest closure. A half cadence ends on the dominant, creating a sense of pause or question. The plagal cadence moves from the fourth chord to the tonic and is gentler, sometimes called the Amen cadence because of its use in hymns. It feels less conclusive than an authentic cadence. The deceptive cadence moves from the dominant to the relative minor, subverting expectation and widely used for surprise or prolonging tension.

A cadence may be perfect, with both chords in root position for maximum strength, or imperfect, affecting its sense of finality. Composers use cadences to shape the listener's sense of phrasing and motion, making them a key tool for tonal navigation. Cadences are the fundamental units of harmonic grammar and represent standardized progressions used to end phrases. They mark structural boundaries in sonata form expositions, developments, and recapitulations, all within the major and minor system in which cadences acquire their meaning and strength.
